title: What Twenty Years of Ramadan Iftars Taught Me About Belonging
script: Narrator: [reflective] Twenty years ago, arriving in this city knowing nobody, I spent my first Ramadan breaking fast alone in a rented room, eating dates from a plastic bag over the sink.

Narrator: [honestly] I remember telling myself it was temporary, a single difficult season I'd simply endure before the loneliness resolved itself naturally, as though belonging were something that accrued automatically with time.
Narrator: [thoughtful] It didn't, of course, not on its own. Belonging, I eventually learned, is considerably less passive than I'd assumed, something built rather than simply waited for.
Narrator: [reflective] The following year, I invited two coworkers I barely knew to break fast at my apartment, an invitation extended with an awkwardness I still cringe recalling.

Narrator: [with feeling] They came, somewhat hesitantly, and something about that first shared iftar, however modest, however overcooked the rice, cracked open a door I hadn't realized was sealed shut.
Narrator: [honestly] Word spread, as these things quietly do, and by the third year, my small apartment could no longer accommodate whoever wanted to attend.

Narrator: [thoughtful] What began as a single lonely man's improvised solution became, gradually and without any deliberate planning on my part, something the neighborhood simply expected each Ramadan.
Narrator: [with feeling] I've hosted widowers with nowhere else to go, students too far from home to travel back, entire families who simply preferred company to their own quiet dining rooms.

Narrator: [gently] What strikes me most, twenty years on, is how little any of this required exceptional generosity on my part, merely the willingness to extend an invitation I once desperately wished someone had extended to me.
Narrator: [reflective] Community, I've come to think, rarely announces itself; it has to be convened, deliberately, by someone willing to absorb the initial awkwardness of asking.
Narrator: [warmly] These days, I rarely have to send the invitations myself. Someone always beats me to it, which feels, after two decades, like the entire quiet point finally realized.
